column8: The WHAT: How has this individual made an impact and delivered results for your project/team/customers this year? Provide 1-2 specific examples.
column9:
Katarina is a solid and capable squad lead and PM. She’s a natural leader and leads us through squad meetings with confidence and clarity.

She’s very easy going and pleasant to work with, and I feel comfortable bringing her issues about everything from issues and questions with experiments and squad operations, to direct personal feedback.

When I went to her with concerns about inefficiencies with our squad’s operations and suggestions for improvements, she was very receptive to my input and feedback. She carried the work forward, put together a document to present to the squad and hosted a meeting where we went through it and agreed on new ways of working. The result of that work has had significant tangible improvements to the squads’s operations.

She’s a great visionary and high-level thinker, and seems to have a great overview over our domain and problem space, and knows where we should focus to make the most impact. I feel confident in her ability to make the right prioritisation calls, which gives me more bandwidth to focus on engineering.
She always comes across as very confident, and I’m curious if there are cases where she’s actually not, and would do well to be more open about her uncertainties and solicit more input from the other squad members.

Katarina has done great alignment work with other squads, Unified Project and Board in particular. That clearly shows up in my interactions with their engineers: they are really open to collaborate with Growth and help us progress with our experimentation in their parts of the product.

I’m wondering if there’s an opportunity for her to delegate some of the typical squad lead tasks. The norm in Unified Design has been for PMs to handle most typical squad lead tasks, but also frequently delegate to the rest of the squad. She should be aware that there’s not necessarily an expectation from the rest of the squad that she handles all of this.

The relationship between her and Even when it comes to squad leadership should be clarified so the squad knows what to expect from each of them.

Katarina often displays a certain lack of sensitivity when it comes to judging what conversations work in large groups (i.e. the whole squad) and not. I’ve given feedback about this on several occasions and she’s very receptive to that. She’s happy to close/shift discussions in the moment or split the meeting into smaller groups when I suggest that, but rarely suggests so herself. Her being more mindful about how we spend the time together as a full squad and when it makes sense to work in smaller groups would help make the squad work more efficiently.

She co authored and helped drive the growth strategy, owned the acquisition roadmap, and led work across discovery, early onboarding, experimentation, and learning. This included navigating significant architectural changes in March that fundamentally altered first time user flows. Despite this, she stayed focused on the core metrics, helped stabilise bounce rates, and contributed to what has been a strong year for acquisition. While these outcomes were the result of collective effort, she played a clear role in holding the strategy together and ensuring the team continued to learn and adapt.

Beyond acquisition, Katarina has contributed meaningfully to shaping how we work. She was involved in operating model work both within growth and more broadly across Forma, proactively engaging leaders from other product areas to improve cross functional alignment. She has also supported and influenced other PMs through mentoring and informal guidance on strategy, discovery, documentation, and prioritisation. Her involvement in PLG collaboration with ACS, including participation in both offsites, has been particularly valuable in aligning PMs across organisations and driving stakeholder buy in beyond the data teams.

column9:
I’ll cover both what I observed and how it showed up in day-to-day work.

I worked with Katarina in the Acquisition squad within Growth. We started off with good alignment on the vision, goals, and priorities.

Given that the squad had already been running for a while and that Katarina had prior experience working with engineers, I expected clearer ways of working to already be in place. In practice, during the first couple of months there was very little structure. We didn’t have consistent planning sessions, retrospectives, or clear team rituals, which made it harder to align on priorities and slowed down execution.

Katarina is quick in her thinking and clearly smart. She is generally good at keeping discussions focused, and when meetings drift, she’s effective at pulling the conversation back to the main point.

One area where improvement is needed is depth of domain understanding and how that showed up in execution. Several experiment descriptions lacked clarity and depth and were not always well thought through in terms of hypotheses, success metrics, or expected impact. This made it harder for the team to confidently execute and evaluate results. While Katarina moves quickly and has strong instincts, it was clear that she was still building deeper context in the domain, and that sometimes speed came at the expense of quality.

Based on my experience working with other Product Managers at Autodesk, there are clear expectations around ownership, domain depth, and bringing structure and clarity to a squad. In this case, those expectations were not consistently met. In particular, gaps in experiment quality, domain context, and team operating structure made it harder for the squad to move efficiently and confidently compared to what I have seen in other teams.

Another area for growth is collaboration style. In multiple situations, even when she wasn’t fully familiar with a topic, Katarina would take control of the discussion and push decisions forward. This sometimes limited input from others who had more context and led to decisions being made without enough exploration.

She also strongly prefers scheduled conversations and advance context, which is understandable. However, in an agile environment, a lot of alignment happens informally and in the moment. This approach made her feel less approachable at times and slowed down collaboration when new questions or requirements came up.

During the four months I was in the squad, it also wasn’t always clear what Katarina’s level of ownership or focus on the Acquisition squad was. She had several parallel responsibilities outside the squad, and at times it was unclear whether the squad had her full attention. This showed up as gaps in product context and less clarity around direction than I would expect from a fully embedded PM.

I raised some of these concerns with Katarina directly on multiple occasions, with the intention of improving how we worked together. These conversations did not lead to meaningful change. Instead, issues were often addressed indirectly rather than through clear, example-based discussion. Over time, this made it harder to build trust and maintain a healthy, open team dynamic.

Overall, while Katarina brings strong analytical thinking and speed, there are clear opportunities for growth in:
• Improving the quality and depth of experiment design
• Building stronger domain context before driving decisions
• Creating space for open, direct feedback
• Being clear about ownership, focus, and availability

Addressing these areas would significantly improve collaboration, trust, and delivery quality within the team.

Cheers
Hesam :)

column9:
Strategy & Problem Definition

Katarina played a major role in defining and prioritizing experiments that informed both our near-term work and longer-term strategy. A strong example is the intent questions and stepper experiment for ACC and non-ACC users. She shaped the problem definition and guided the squad through a structured discovery process that allowed us to identify how different user segments (ACC vs. AUM) respond to friction during onboarding.

Her leadership helped us determine that for high-intent users, the revised questions and stepper introduced “positive friction”—screening out low-intent users early and allowing higher-quality users to progress further into the funnel. In contrast, the same experience created unnecessary friction for ACC users, negatively impacting their conversion. These insights clarified that we need differentiated onboarding solutions depending on the user entry point, which meaningfully influenced our growth strategy.


Cross-Functional Alignment

Earlier this year, our squad experienced significant overlap with the Unified Project team, creating confusion around ownership of updates, conflicting experiments, and changes that were difficult to track. Katarina proactively resolved these challenges by establishing cross-product alignment and creating weekly syncs with Unified Project. Using PLG principles, she demonstrated the impact of our work and built momentum around experimentation across product areas.
Her influence is evident today: Unified Project and Board squads now run their own experiments, participate in shared roadmap alignment, and use experimentation as a core part of their process. Katarina played a central role in expanding this culture of experimentation, and her work continues to enable smoother collaboration and cross-team visibility.
